Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

data.title: Rethinking Soft Tokens for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37391, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel generation by predicting and committing multiple tokens at each denoising step, yet they can generate individually plausible but mutually inconsistent tokens. Recent work shows that \emph{soft tokens} can mitigate this issue by representing uncertain positions with continuous embeddings built from the model's predictive distribution at the previous decoding step. However, although soft tokens are commonly understood as preserving predictive uncertainty, how soft-token feedback improves parallel decoding has not been systematically examined. In this paper, we investigate this question in frozen pretrained DLMs to examine soft-token feedback without the effects of additional training. To construct soft-token inputs in a training-free setting, we identify a geometric mismatch between conventional soft-token construction and the pretrained embedding space. Based on this observation, we propose a training-free, geometry-aware construction of soft tokens. Our analysis of soft-token feedback suggests that uncertainty preservation alone does not fully explain how it reshapes subsequent predictions. To better explain how soft-token feedback improves parallel decoding, we provide empirical evidence that it favors coherent token sequences. Across four pretrained DLMs and four math and code benchmarks, our method outperforms standard parallel decoding and a training-free Euclidean soft-token baseline. Code: https://github.com/kodaikawamura/rethinking-soft-tokens

data.title: UniRank: A Multi-Agent Calibration Pipeline for Estimating University Rankings from Anonymized Bibliometric Signals

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18824, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: We present UniRank, a multi-agent LLM pipeline that estimates university positions across global ranking systems using only publicly available bibliometric data from OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar. The system employs a three-stage architecture: (a) zero-shot estimation from anonymized institutional metrics, (b) per-system tool-augmented calibration against real ranked universities, and (c) final synthesis. Critically, institutions are anonymized -- names, countries, DOIs, paper titles, and collaboration countries are all redacted -- and their actual ranks are hidden from the calibration tools during evaluation, preventing LLM memorization from confounding results. On the Times Higher Education (THE) World University Rankings ($n=352$), the system achieves MAE = 251.5 rank positions, Median AE = 131.5, PNMAE = 12.03%, Spearman $\rho = 0.769$, Kendall $\tau = 0.591$, hit rate @50 = 20.7%, hit rate @100 = 39.8%, and a Memorization Index of exactly zero (no exact-match zero-width predictions among all 352 universities). The systematic positive-signed error (+190.1 positions, indicating the system consistently predicts worse ranks than actual) and monotonic performance degradation from elite tier (MAE = 60.5, hit@100 = 90.5%) to tail tier (MAE = 328.2, hit@100 = 20.8%) provide strong evidence that the pipeline performs genuine analytical reasoning rather than recalling memorized rankings. A live demo is available at https://unirank.scinito.ai .

data.title: On the Calibration of Large Language Models and Alignment

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.13240, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: As large language models attract increasing attention and find widespread application, concurrent challenges of reliability also arise at the same time. Confidence calibration, an effective analysis method for gauging the reliability of deep models, serves as a crucial tool for assessing and improving their reliability. However, such investigation has been comparatively underexplored. In this work, we conduct a systematic examination of the calibration of aligned language models throughout the entire construction process, including pretraining and alignment training. At each stage, we investigate how different training settings, such as parameter scales and training data, affect model calibration. To thoroughly assess model calibration, we evaluate models on three most concerned aspects: generation, factuality and understanding. Our work sheds light on whether popular LLMs are well-calibrated and how the training process influences model calibration.

data.title: Large Language and Multimodal Models in Archaeological Science: A Review

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.3390/electronics14224507?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics14224507, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Models (LMMs) are significantly influencing scientific research, including archaeology—a discipline dealing with uniquely complex, multimodal data. This comprehensive review systematically examines recent (2023+) applications of LLMs/LMMs in archaeology, covering ancient texts, artifacts, field data, and knowledge graphs. While current applications are often exploratory and fragmented, they demonstrate substantial potential for addressing long-standing archaeological challenges such as data heterogeneity, knowledge integration, and interpretive complexity. We argue that archaeology serves as a valuable “proving ground” for next-generation AI technologies due to its distinctive data characteristics (multimodal heterogeneity, sparsity, uncertainty) and high demands for robust knowledge reasoning and interpretability. This review critically analyzes technical approaches including fine-tuning methods (LoRA, PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and recent advances (RAFT, LongRoPE, Phi-3-mini) that enable efficient local deployment. We examine data, knowledge, technological, and ethical challenges, distinguishing between issues generic to machine learning and those specific to Transformer-based LLMs in heritage contexts. This review concludes by identifying prioritized future research directions for integrated “AI Archaeology,” emphasizing responsible AI principles and human-in-the-loop frameworks. This study offers cross-disciplinary insights for fostering deep, synergistic, and ethically sound AI integration within archaeological science and broader cultural heritage applications.

data.title: Few-Shot Learning in Video and 3D Object Detection: A Survey

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17079, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Few-shot learning (FSL) and data-efficient learning paradigms enable object detection models to recognize novel classes from minimally annotated examples, addressing expensive data-labeling challenges. This systematic survey examines recent advances in few-shot, semi-supervised, sparsely-supervised, and weakly-supervised approaches for video and 3D object detection, focusing on developments through foundation models and vision-language model integration. For video object detection, techniques including tube proposals, temporal matching networks, motion-guided approaches, and temporal consistency-based semi-supervised methods utilize spatiotemporal relationships for efficient novel class adaptation, with recent architectures achieving substantial gains from 33 to 48 average precision in few-shot scenarios. For 3D object detection, specialized approaches address point cloud sparsity and texture limitations through uncertainty-aware methods, geometric learning, and multimodal fusion, with sparsely-supervised techniques achieving competitive performance using only 2% of annotations, enabling practical deployment in autonomous driving and robotics. The survey analyzes methodological advances including meta-learning, transfer learning, pseudo-label generation, contrastive instance mining, and foundation model integration across applications spanning autonomous driving, surveillance, robotics, industrial control, and medical imaging. By examining developments across multiple supervision paradigms, this work highlights data-efficient learning’s potential for minimizing annotation requirements and enabling robust real-world deployment across temporal, spatial, and multimodal domains.

data.title: Cataloging cysteines in ECOD domains using a protein language model

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.64898/2026.05.13.724926?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.05.13.724926, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Cysteine is among the most chemically versatile residues in the proteome, existing in three competing functional states: metal coordination, covalent disulfide bonding, and bioactive free thiols. Although these states can be readily assigned from experimentally determined protein structures using simple geometric criteria, accurately annotating them from predicted structures remains challenging. To bridge the gap between predicted structures and functional interpretation, we developed TriCyP (Tri-state Cysteine Predictor), an efficient two-layer neural network built on ESM-2 protein language model embeddings. On an independent benchmark set, TriCyP achieves near-perfect accuracy (AUROC = 0.99) and outperforms existing approaches for predicting both disulfide bonding and metal coordination. We applied TriCyP to classify 2.7 million cysteine residues across 0.9 million ECOD F70 representative domains. The resulting proteome-scale landscape recapitulates established biological patterns. Cysteines are enriched in eukaryotes: disulfide-bonded states are concentrated in extracellular proteins, and metal-coordinating cysteines peak in nuclear proteins owing to the abundance of zinc-finger transcription factors. We further demonstrate the utility of cysteine-state annotation through two pilot studies. First, predicted disulfide-forming cysteines lacking a corresponding structural partner in AlphaFold models may identify either regions of elevated structural uncertainty or latent inter-protein disulfide bonds that stabilize protein-protein interactions. Second, systematic analysis of known and predicted metal-coordinating cysteines across ECOD homologous groups uncovers previously unrecognized metal-binding protein families. This proteome-wide catalog of cysteine states is available as a community resource (http://prodata.swmed.edu/tricyp) and will be integrated into future ECOD releases.

data.title: VMBES: A Vision-Language-Guided Multi-UAV Framework for Bandwidth-Efficient Situational Awareness

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1109/SysCon66367.2026.11503574?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1109/SysCon66367.2026.11503574, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Achieving reliable situational awareness in disaster environments requires rapid identification of collapsed structures, blocked access routes, hazardous zones, and potential survivors. Although autonomous UAVs offer fast and flexible data collection, existing solutions remain constrained by bandwidth limitations, reliance on ground-based processing, and a lack of multiagent semantic coordination. Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have enhanced visual understanding through open vocabulary recognition and contextual reasoning; however, most VLM-enabled UAV frameworks rely on cloud offloading and uninterrupted connectivity, which are often unavailable in postdisaster settings. Furthermore, current autonomous UAV methods typically operate as isolated agents or exchange raw sensor data without aggregating semantic knowledge across platforms or integrating human operator cues, limiting their ability to prioritize high-value regions and adapt to rapidly evolving conditions. This paper introduces VMBES, a vision-language guided multiUAV framework designed for bandwidth-efficient situational awareness in communication-constrained disaster environments. VMBES executes semantic inference entirely onboard each UAV, enabling the system to function independently of ground infrastructure. The framework consists of three tightly coupled modules: onboard semantic perception, bandwidth-aware semantic fusion across UAVs, and receding-horizon planning that jointly optimizes motion, sensing, and communication under energy and bandwidth constraints. A distributed semantic belief map allows UAVs to consolidate evidence from diverse viewpoints, incorporate human guidance, and systematically reduce uncertainty over mission-critical assets. We evaluate VMBES using high-fidelity simulations and outdoor field experiments on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX-based UAV platform, comparing against centralized, coverage-based, and learning-driven baselines. Results show that VMBES maintains robust performance under strict bandwidth limits while significantly accelerating the discovery of critical assets, demonstrating its value for resilient disaster response operations.

data.title: Large language models in healthcare quality management: a European perspective on process automation and compliance

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13062252, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming back-office quality management processes in European healthcare systems through automation of compliance monitoring, quality assurance, and process optimization without direct patient interaction. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from recent systematic reviews and implementation studies (2023-2025) examining LLM deployment within the European regulatory framework encompassing the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation EU 2024/1689). Current research demonstrates meaningful efficiency gains: individual studies of AI-assisted documentation tools report improvements ranging from modest increases in documentation speed to reductions in processing time approaching 50%, while broader policy analyses estimate administrative workload reductions of up to 30% through digital health and AI solutions. Clinical trial applications show particular maturity, with LLM-generated informed consent forms demonstrating improved readability (76% vs. 67%) without compromising accuracy. However, critical gaps persist between research achievements and practical deployment. Analysis of 519 evaluation studies reveals that only 5% utilized real patient care data, while 95% focused exclusively on accuracy metrics to the neglect of fairness (16%), deployment readiness (5%), and calibration (1%). No LLM-based quality management system has yet received regulatory clearance, and implementation science frameworks remain underdeveloped. We propose a risk-stratified implementation framework emphasizing process-oriented applications—standard operating procedure automation, audit documentation, deviation management, and compliance monitoring—that avoid medical device classification while capturing substantial operational benefits. Advanced methodological approaches including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architectures, digital twin integration, and natural language processing-based pattern recognition offer pathways toward comprehensive quality intelligence platforms. The convergence of LLMs with emerging technologies such as knowledge graphs, digital twin architectures and multimodal analysis creates opportunities for predictive quality management that anticipates rather than merely documents quality-relevant events. Evidence supports deployment in administrative quality processes, with particular potential for applications that redirect human expertise from documentation toward quality improvement activities, though current evidence derives predominantly from non-European healthcare contexts and simulated or limited-scope settings. Success requires adapted validation methodologies addressing LLM non-determinism, robust governance structures, and comprehensive change management that maintains the high standards European healthcare systems demand.

data.title: Assessment of ChatGPT-3.5's Knowledge in Oncology: Comparative Study with ASCO-SEP Benchmarks

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11041475, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Background ChatGPT (Open AI) is a state-of-the-art large language model that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to address questions across diverse topics. The American Society of Clinical Oncology Self-Evaluation Program (ASCO-SEP) created a comprehensive educational program to help physicians keep up to date with the many rapid advances in the field. The question bank consists of multiple choice questions addressing the many facets of cancer care, including diagnosis, treatment, and supportive care. As ChatGPT applications rapidly expand, it becomes vital to ascertain if the knowledge of ChatGPT-3.5 matches the established standards that oncologists are recommended to follow. Objective This study aims to evaluate whether ChatGPT-3.5’s knowledge aligns with the established benchmarks that oncologists are expected to adhere to. This will furnish us with a deeper understanding of the potential applications of this tool as a support for clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted a systematic assessment of the performance of ChatGPT-3.5 on the ASCO-SEP, the leading educational and assessment tool for medical oncologists in training and practice. Over 1000 multiple choice questions covering the spectrum of cancer care were extracted. Questions were categorized by cancer type or discipline, with subcategorization as treatment, diagnosis, or other. Answers were scored as correct if ChatGPT-3.5 selected the answer as defined by ASCO-SEP. Results Overall, ChatGPT-3.5 achieved a score of 56.1% (583/1040) for the correct answers provided. The program demonstrated varying levels of accuracy across cancer types or disciplines. The highest accuracy was observed in questions related to developmental therapeutics (8/10; 80% correct), while the lowest accuracy was observed in questions related to gastrointestinal cancer (102/209; 48.8% correct). There was no significant difference in the program’s performance across the predefined subcategories of diagnosis, treatment, and other (P=.16, which is greater than .05). Conclusions This study evaluated ChatGPT-3.5’s oncology knowledge using the ASCO-SEP, aiming to address uncertainties regarding AI tools like ChatGPT in clinical decision-making. Our findings suggest that while ChatGPT-3.5 offers a hopeful outlook for AI in oncology, its present performance in ASCO-SEP tests necessitates further refinement to reach the requisite competency levels. Future assessments could explore ChatGPT’s clinical decision support capabilities with real-world clinical scenarios, its ease of integration into medical workflows, and its potential to foster interdisciplinary collaboration and patient engagement in health care settings.

data.title: Automated Judging of LLM-based Smart Contract Security Auditors

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1109/ICBC64466.2025.11114647?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1109/ICBC64466.2025.11114647, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The rise of Large Language Model-based smart contract auditors, supplementing manual audits, lacks standardized evaluation methods. This creates considerable uncertainty about their reliability and effectiveness in identifying vulnerabilities. This gap is particularly critical as smart contract exploits continue to result in billion-dollar losses and the complexity of blockchain systems grows exponentially. Our research introduces smartJudge, a comprehensive evaluation framework that systematically assesses the capabilities of LLM-based smart contract auditors through multi-dimensional analysis. To develop smartJudge, we first created an agenticRAG architecture that leverages agents to acquire in-depth knowledge and build expertise on smart contract auditing, vulnerabilities, and best practices. We then developed a distilled LLM judge model that efficiently processes auditor outputs through strategic evaluation points to evaluate how well auditors detect vulnerability patterns, understand security research, and identify complex vulnerability chains. Finally, we constructed a benchmark suite with evaluation metrics providing a standardized way to measure auditor performance across diverse vulnerability types. Testing smartJudge on the representative LLM-based auditors revealed critical gaps in vulnerability detection capabilities, particularly in complex attack vectors and novel exploit patterns. Our framework provides insights for improving automated auditing tools and establishes the first systematic methodology for evaluating LLM-based smart contract auditors, addressing a crucial bottleneck in blockchain security tools.

data.title: Modeling Clinical Uncertainty in Radiology Reports: from Explicit Uncertainty Markers to Implicit Reasoning Pathways

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.04506, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Radiology reports are invaluable for clinical decision-making and hold great potential for automated analysis when structured into machine-readable formats. These reports often contain uncertainty, which we categorize into two distinct types: (i) Explicit uncertainty reflects doubt about the presence or absence of findings, conveyed through hedging phrases. These vary in meaning depending on the context, making rule-based systems insufficient to quantify the level of uncertainty for specific findings; (ii) Implicit uncertainty arises when radiologists omit parts of their reasoning, recording only key findings or diagnoses. Here, it is often unclear whether omitted findings are truly absent or simply unmentioned for brevity. We address these challenges with a two-part framework. We quantify explicit uncertainty by creating an expert-validated, LLM-based reference ranking of common hedging phrases, and mapping each finding to a probability value based on this reference. In addition, we model implicit uncertainty through an expansion framework that systematically adds characteristic sub-findings derived from expert-defined diagnostic pathways for 14 common diagnoses. Using these methods, we release Lunguage++, an expanded, uncertainty-aware version of the Lunguage benchmark of fine-grained structured radiology reports. This enriched resource enables uncertainty-aware image classification, faithful diagnostic reasoning, and new investigations into the clinical impact of diagnostic uncertainty.

data.abstract: An important issue to consider is the training time, as it can have a considerable influence on the set of stories generated, due to factors such as uncertainty, diversity, and narrative coherence. This paper presents a systematic analysis of the dynamics of predictive entropy at different times and random seeds, studying the interaction of entropy with lexical diversity, repetition, semantic consistency, and entity continuity in probabilistic language generation models. A comparative evaluation of recurrent and attention-based architectures is performed using linguistic metrics. Predictive entropy was reduced by 32.4% (LSTM) and 28.7% (Transformer). LexDiv obtained 0.71 ± 0.03 and Self-BLEU obtained 0.42 ± 0.02, suggesting greater confidence in the model. However, it should be noted that a greater reduction in entropy may be associated with lower lexical diversity and higher Self-BLEU scores. This indicates a trade-off between confidence and expressiveness in probabilistic language models. The entropy term encourages smoother probability distributions and reduces premature mode collapse during Adam optimization. Ltotal=LCE−λH(p(y|x) aims to improve stability, reduce random initialization, and enable the generation of adaptable narratives, which may be relevant for neurodiversity-oriented narratives.

data.title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37684, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.

data.abstract: We introduce Self-Anchoring Calibration Drift (SACD), a hypothesized tendency for large language models (LLMs) to show systematic changes in expressed confidence when building iteratively on their own prior outputs across multi-turn conversations. We report an empirical study comparing three frontier models -- Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.2 -- across 150 questions spanning factual, technical, and open-ended domains, using three conditions: single-turn baseline (A), multi-turn self-anchoring (B), and independent repetition control (C). Results reveal a complex, model-heterogeneous pattern that partially diverges from pre-registered hypotheses. data.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Safety Data Extraction

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11204, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Accurate extraction of structured information from Safety Data Sheets (SDS) remains challenging in industrial safety due to heterogeneous document formats and the limitations of traditional rule-based methods. This study benchmarks state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) for automated SDS data extraction, comparing text-based and multimodal processing pipelines. We systematically evaluate four models: Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Llama 3.1-70B, across three prompting strategies: zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought. The evaluation framework assessed accuracy, latency, and cost across more than 50,000 extracted data fields. Results show that text-based extraction consistently outperforms multimodal processing across all metrics. Gemini 1.5 Pro combined with a Chain-of-Thought prompt achieved the highest accuracy (84%), outperforming GPT-4o (81%) and Claude 3.7 Sonnet (79%). However, no model surpassed the 90% accuracy threshold commonly required for reliable real-world deployment. These findings indicate that general-purpose LLMs are not yet robust enough for unsupervised industrial use, though performance suggests strong potential with task-specific fine-tuning. Future research should focus on domain-adapted training, model calibration, and the integration of Human-in-the-Loop verification to ensure safety-critical reliability.

data.title: Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic-Temperature Distillation for Efficient Biomedical Sentence Classification

Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Domain-specific pretrained language models (PLMs) have set new benchmarks in biomedical text mining, yet their immense computational demands hinder deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a viable compression path, but the optimal integration of diverse distillation signals for specialized biomedical tasks remains underexplored. This paper proposes an Adaptive Multi-Objective Knowledge Distillation framework designed to transfer task-specific expertise from PubMedBERT to a lightweight MiniLM for GAD sentence classification. Our framework features an entropy-guided dynamic-temperature mechanism that adjustably softens teacher logits based on predictive uncertainty, complemented by multi-level feature alignment and relational knowledge transfer. Systematic experiments demonstrate that the distilled student significantly outperforms the non-distilled baseline, achieving an Accuracy of 77.22, F1-score of 80.41, and ROC-AUC of 83.41. Detailed ablation and parameter studies reveal that while logit-level response matching drives primary performance gains, feature-level alignment acts as a sensitive regularizer that requires precise weighting to avoid over-constraining the student’s representational capacity. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for balancing supervised learning with multi-objective teacher guidance in high-precision biomedical NLP applications.

data.abstract: Satellite and spacecraft telemetry systems produce vast amounts of multivariate time-series data, which are critical for spacecraft health monitoring, fault diagnosis, and mission assurance. Modern developments in artificial intelligence and deep learning have led to dramatic improvements in anomaly detection performance. Yet, many approaches still struggle with explainability, causal reasoning, the lack of standardized benchmarks, high computational cost, and limited on-board deployment feasibility. This paper presents a systematic literature review of AI-based telemetry anomaly detection, focusing on deep learning, explainable AI, transformer learning, graph neural networks and emerging language-model-inspired techniques. We conducted a systematic review of a curated corpus of 47 primary studies, accessed through Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Springer Nature Link and Taylor & Francis Online. The review followed PRISMA guidelines and incorporated thematic synthesis, taxonomy development, quality assessment, dataset mapping, and research-gap analysis. The review shows a clear trend from traditional machine learning to recurrent neural networks, autoencoder-based methods, transformer-based temporal learning and hybrid frameworks. It also stresses the increasing importance of explainability and context reasoning for autonomous spacecraft operations. We propose a conceptual framework to address key gaps and limitations across transformer learning, graph causal reasoning, explainable AI components, retrieval-augmented language models, and uncertainty-aware intelligence. This framework can support the development of more interpretable, autonomous spacecraft health-monitoring systems.

data.title: L26/P-419 Can AI advise on oocyte freezing? A multi-model analysis of the informational completeness, reliability and reproducibility of large language models’ responses on common patient queries

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1093/humrep/deag083.753?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1093/humrep/deag083.753, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract:
Do popular large language models (LLMs) provide informationally complete, reliable and reproducible advice to patients considering oocyte cryopreservation?
 
 
 
 LLM responses generally demonstrated sufficient informational completeness, although with considerable variation across models, problematic reliability with frequent hallucinations, and low reproducibility with substantial intra-inter-model variability.
 
 
 
 Oocyte cryopreservation is increasingly used to preserve reproductive potential, however the evidence supporting reliable patient counseling remains limited. Concurrently, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has led many patients to seek medical advice from LLMs (usually through the use of chatbots). To date, no systematic critical appraisal of the counseling information provided by these models has been conducted. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically appraise the informational completeness, reliability and reproducibility of the responses generated by different LLMs, using prompts designed as hypothetical patient queries, to simulate counseling for patients considering or undergoing oocyte cryopreservation.
 
 
 
 Fifteen LLM models from six LLM families (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, MetaAI) were appraised in January 2026. For each LLM, free and paid versions (with standard and extended thinking modes) were evaluated. Standardized prompts inquiring on the probability of ≥ 1 live birth were used, including four age scenarios (30, 34, 38, 44) combined with four number-of-cryopreserved-oocytes scenarios (5, 10, 15, 25). Each prompt was submitted twice, in different sessions to ensure independence (480 observations).
 
 
 
 Two reviewers independently assessed each response for informational completeness (uncertainty communication, interpretation aid, limitations), reliability (hallucinations, encouragement for medical consultation), and reproducibility (intra-&inter-model agreement). Associations of these characteristics with LLM family and tier were tested using Chi-square. Intra-model and inter-model agreement in live birth probability estimates of identical prompts was evaluated using mean absolute and relative differences, and coefficient of variation (CV). All analyses were performed with STATA 18 and p ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
 
 
 
 The word count of each response ranged from 123 to 812. Most responses communicated uncertainty (94.0%, 95%CI:91.5%-95.8%), included interpretation aid (86.7%, 95%CI:83.6%-89.7%) and acknowledged limitations (81.7%, 95%CI:78.2%-85.1%), albeit differing significantly by model family (p < 0.001). Specific references appeared in just over 50% of the responses (54.4%, 95%CI:49.9%-58.8%), yet only 41% (95%CI: 35.0–47.2%) of these were free of hallucinations, which also differed significantly by model family (p < 0.001). Encouragement to consult a physician was present in only 53.8% (95%CI:49.3%-58.2%) of the responses. The LLM model tier (basic, advanced, expert) was positively associated with the inclusion of interpretation aid and limitations as well as the probability of remaining free of hallucinations (p < 0.001). However, it was negatively associated with the inclusion of uncertainty communication and encouragement for medical consultation (p < 0.001).
 Substantial intra-model variability was observed in live birth probability estimates between identical prompts (mean absolute difference=5.0±6.0pp, range:2.6-8.3 and mean relative difference=15.2%±18.9%, range:4.3%-23.7%), with mean CV 10.8%±13.4%, and only 45% (95%CI:38.8%-51.3%) of the responses fully consistent, differing significantly by model family (p < 0.001). Inter-model variability was also substantial (mean absolute difference=34.6±9.9pp, range:17.5-60.0 and mean relative difference=116.8%±97.2%, range:24.9%-300.9%), with CV across all LLMs of 25.0%±21.9% and the poorest agreement in clinically challenging scenarios (advanced age, fewer oocytes).
 
 
 
 This study evaluated the most widely used LLMs in January 2026, which precludes generalizability to future models. Not all clinical scenarios could be evaluated, however sufficient coverage was provided. Only two runs per prompt were performed for efficiency reasons (480 observations), however, this still allowed detection of substantial intra-model inconsistencies.
 
 
 
 These findings underscore the substantial variability in the informational completeness, reliability and reproducibility of LLM-generated counseling for women considering oocyte cryopreservation. Clinicians and patients should exercise caution when interpreting AI-generated information and prioritize evidence-based, professionally validated sources, to minimize misinformation and potential clinical harm.
